The fair had used equipment from science classrooms, the art room, and the small greenhouse, and the boxes had been brought back in several trips because the cart could not fit through the greenhouse door. The main return was due Monday morning, but Ms. Chen wanted us to count everything on Friday so teachers could report anything still missing before the weekend. The return included materials that belonged to different departments, so we kept the labels visible and did not combine items just because they looked alike.

First, we cleared the long table by the sinks and put down a clean paper sheet for small pieces. The green crate held six hand lenses, three plastic trays, a roll of copper tape, and a sealed packet of bean seeds. The packet was still sealed, and Ms. Chen said it should go back to the greenhouse cabinet rather than to the science storeroom. The blue tub held two pairs of safety goggles. One had a loose strap, and the other had a scratched lens. The goggles with the scratched lens were usable for the demonstration but not for student use, so we put them in a separate bag with a note. The three thermometers were all there, and the red one still had its paper tag around the stem. We also found a glass jar with no lid and a lid with no matching jar, and kept them together in a box marked “Needs checking.”

1. Say the item, the location, and the person responsible for checking it. The small magnifiers came from Room 12, and Ms. Patel checked the count. The plastic trays came from the art room, and Mr. Lewis checked those. The seed packet and the watering gauge came from the greenhouse, and Ms. Chen checked them. The library aide will sign the return sheet because she is covering the front desk while the custodian checks the gym inventory. Ms. Chen will keep the duplicate copy until the aide has signed, and then the original goes into the office envelope. We wrote the corrected responsibility in the margin before making the final copy.

We counted eight extension leads, but only seven were in the coil bag. One was on the display table beside the model volcano, and Mr. Lewis brought it over before we finished the count. The orange lead had a small split near the plug, and we did not test it. We marked it “Do not use” and left it on the table for the science department chair to inspect. The power strip had six outlets, and its switch worked when we checked it. There was also a cardboard sign that said, “Please do not move the model until the glue is dry.” The volcano was dry by Friday, but the sign had a handwritten note on the back about returning the black gravel to Room 12, so we kept the note with the model instead of throwing it away.

Ms. Chen read the label on the storage cabinet aloud: “Return the lenses in their cloth sleeves and leave the calibration card in the top drawer.” The sleeves were in a small envelope in the cabinet, and there were five of them although we had counted six hand lenses, so we checked the science prep room and found the last sleeve in a drying rack. We did not find the calibration card in the top drawer at first. It was inside the blue folder on the shelf above the cabinet. Ms. Chen moved it back into the drawer after checking the number printed on it. The drawer also held two old batteries that were not part of the fair equipment, and we left them there rather than adding them to the return list.

For the art room return, Mr. Lewis counted twelve brushes and nine mixing palettes. The brushes were dry, but two palettes still had a thin layer of blue paint, so he put those beside the sink with a note for the art teacher. The paper lantern frames were stacked flat with tissue between them, and one frame had a bent corner. Mr. Lewis said he would show it to the art teacher before deciding whether it could be stored with the others. The greenhouse watering gauge was clean and its scale was readable, but the plastic clip was cracked. Ms. Chen said if the greenhouse teacher wants to reuse the gauge, the teacher should replace the clip first; otherwise, it should stay in the small repair box until the next equipment review. We attached a note stating that condition to the gauge.

Before we closed the equipment room, we checked the return sheet against the labels one more time. The entries for the Room 12 materials were on the first page, and the art and greenhouse entries were on the second page. The blue tub and the bag with the damaged goggles had separate lines so no one would mistake them for ordinary usable supplies. We put the sealed seed packet in a dry envelope and placed it on the greenhouse shelf. The jar and loose lid remained in the “Needs checking” box because we could not tell whether they belonged together. The orange extension lead stayed out of the coil bag, and the note about the volcano gravel stayed with the model.

I carried the office envelope to the front desk but did not leave it there because the library aide was helping a parent and had not signed yet. Ms. Chen kept the duplicate copy, and I took the original back to the equipment room for the night. The aide can sign it Monday morning before the returned supplies are distributed, and the custodian can check the gym inventory separately. If the office is still locked when we arrive, the original should remain with Ms. Chen until the desk opens. We left the table clear except for the bagged goggles, the orange lead, the repair box, and the model with its handwritten gravel note, and Ms. Chen locked the equipment room after we checked that the greenhouse shelf was dry."}]
